pages.text: EXHIBIT A

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
v. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

SECOND AMENDED AND SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT
DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

1. On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy
against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in
September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the
motion.

2. When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by
Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child
sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to
dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

3. I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning

those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name,

“Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have
never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed
motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

4. I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and
delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline
report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior
lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

5. I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify,
maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense
may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the
motions is to be determined.

6. That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:

“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National

Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its
written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1)
Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-
level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the
present.”

7. So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal
name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted
CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J.
Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service?
Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery,
or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where

did the urgency come from?

8. I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against
all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional
infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters
said and to whom.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE

9. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1).
Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

10. This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims
for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting
words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation,
approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of
the same case or controversy.

11. This Court has independent subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)
(1) over Counts I,  II, III, and VI, which are asserted only against Hall and NCMEC. Plaintiff is a
citizen of the State of Florida. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than
Florida and is a citizen of that State. NCMEC is a Virginia non-profit corporation with its principal
place of business in Alexandria, Virginia, and is a citizen of Virginia. Complete diversity exists
between Plaintiff and each Defendant against whom those Counts are asserted. The amount in
controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

12. Venue is proper in this district under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2). A substantial part of
the events giving rise to the claims occurred here. Hall prepared or approved, signed, and issued

the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s office in Alexandria, Virginia, within the Alexandria

Division of this district. The letters were transmitted to Plaintiff’s commercial mail-receiving
address in Alexandria, Virginia, where they were opened and processed.

13. This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Hall under Virginia Code § 8.01-
328.1(A)(3). Hall performed the challenged acts in Virginia. She prepared or approved, signed,
issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s Alexandria
headquarters. The first third-party publication alleged in this Complaint occurred in Alexandria,
when the commercial mail-receiving agency opened, reviewed, and scanned the letters. Each
claim against Hall arises from her Virginia conduct.

14. This Court has general personal jurisdiction over NCMEC, a Virginia corporation
with its principal place of business in Alexandria, Virginia. This Court also has specific personal
jurisdiction over NCMEC under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). The April 22, 2026 letters
were prepared or approved, signed, and issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters, and each
claim against NCMEC arises from that Virginia conduct.

15. This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Meta Platforms, Inc. under
Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3) and the conspiracy-based attribution of forum contacts.
Sections N through Q allege the conspiracy. Meta knowingly participated through one or more
authorized representatives or intermediaries. NCMEC and Hall committed the Virginia acts
alleged in this Complaint in furtherance of that conspiracy. Meta received the April 9, 2026
materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department in Alexandria, Virginia. The understanding
alleged in Section N contemplated that Hall would issue the case-specific correspondence from
that Virginia office. Plaintiff’s claim against Meta arises from those Virginia acts.

16. The exercise of personal jurisdiction over each Defendant comports with the Due

Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

PARTIES

17. Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, also known as Jay Ballentine, is an adult citizen of
the State of Florida. At all relevant times Plaintiff maintained a mailing address at 1520 Belle
View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307. A commercial mail-receiving agency
operates that address and is authorized to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf.

18. Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) is a
Virginia non-profit corporation. Its principal place of business is 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite
125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. NCMEC operates the CyberTipline under federal authorization
in connection with 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. At all relevant times NCMEC employed Defendant Katie
Hall as its Corporate Counsel. Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in
response to claimed legal process. NCMEC is sued for its own conduct, undertaken through Hall
and one or more additional personnel. NCMEC is also sued vicariously for Hall’s conduct within
the scope of her employment.

19. Defendant Katie Hall is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Corporate
Counsel of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On
information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State.
Hall prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026
letters. Hall is sued individually for her own tortious conduct.

20. Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) is a Delaware corporation with its
principal place of business in Menlo Park, California. Meta was a defendant in the 376 Action and
in the 286 Action at all relevant times. Meta is an electronic service provider subject to the
reporting duties of 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

21. Meta owns and operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

22. Defendants John/Jane Does 1-6 are persons not yet identified who participated in
the communications, authorization, approval, preparation, or transmission alleged in this
Complaint. Their roles include: the Meta representative or representatives who communicated
with NCMEC concerning Plaintiff, the identifiers, the intended subpoenas, or the two federal
actions; any Accenture representative who knowingly joined or implemented the understanding
alleged in this Complaint; the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026
letters; and any intermediary, including counsel or other agents acting for Meta, Accenture, or
NCMEC, through whom the alleged communications occurred. Meta, Accenture, NCMEC, and
their representatives hold the records that identify the Doe Defendants. Plaintiff will seek leave to
amend when those identities are ascertained.

SCOPE OF ALLEGATIONS

23. This Complaint predicates no liability on the filing of any motion, brief, or other
paper in any court. Court filings identified here are alleged solely as facts establishing timing,
notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions. The claims do not challenge NCMEC’s receipt,
maintenance, or lawful referral of CyberTipline reports. The claims challenge the extra-judicial
agreement alleged below and the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of
external legal correspondence that falsely invoked compulsory process and served the litigation-
directed purposes alleged below. No claim against Meta seeks liability for the July 4, 2022
account-level enforcement, for any content-related decision, for any failure to restore Plaintiff’s
account, or for any treatment of third-party content. Those matters are alleged only to establish the
subject matter of the pending federal actions, Defendants’ knowledge, Meta’s interest in whether
a CyberTipline report exists, and the testimony Defendants sought to deter. The same is true of the

memorandum, motion to stay, and opposition filed in the 1341 Action and the August 13, 2026

filing in the 376 Action, each identified in Section O. Each is alleged as an admission and as a fact
establishing timing, coordination, and knowledge. None is conduct on which any claim rests.

FACTS
A. The Federal Proceedings and Plaintiff’s Role as Party and Prospective

Witness

24. Plaintiff filed the 286 Action on February 9, 2026. Plaintiff filed the 376 Action on
February 17, 2026. Each action was pending in a court of the United States at all relevant times.

25. The defendants in the 376 Action included Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and
Genpact Limited. Accenture is a limited liability partnership that provides platform policy
enforcement services to Meta. The defendants in the 286 Action included Meta, Devin S.
Anderson, and Christopher W. Keegan. Kirkland & Ellis LLP (“Kirkland”) represented Anderson
and Keegan. Accenture, Anderson, Keegan, TaskUs, Inc., Genpact Limited, Kirkland, Orrick,
Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP (“Orrick”), Diana M. Fassbender, and Mariana Chapleau are not
defendants here. Their conduct is alleged only to establish chronology, notice, knowledge, or the
conduct of the Defendants, including the Doe Defendants.

26. Both actions arise from one event. On July 4, 2022, Meta issued an account-level
enforcement notice against Plaintiff’s Facebook account. That notice interrupted Plaintiff’s ability
to perform third-party contracts through the account.

27. Plaintiff proceeded pro se in both actions. Every act of prosecution depended on
Plaintiff’s personal capacity and participation: discovery, deposition examination, briefing, and
appearance.

28. Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions. He expected to testify under
oath, at deposition and at trial, concerning his account history, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event,

the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

29. The dockets of the 376 Action and the 286 Action were publicly accessible through

the federal Public Access to Court Electronic Records system.
B. The Contested CyberTipline Question

30. One question has been contested since October 2025: whether Meta, or any person
acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline
report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers.

31. Before April 22, 2026, no CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff had been
identified, produced, or attributed to any provider in any forum.

32.  Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a
single early request for admission. The request asked whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report
regarding Plaintiff’s account. The court denied the motion.

33. From that denial forward, the defendants in the 376 Action knew what Plaintiff’s
discovery would target: the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report.

34. The operative complaint in the 376 Action alleged that Meta filed no CyberTipline
report. Its prayer sought a declaration that no CyberTipline report was filed regarding the July 4,
2022 enforcement event.

35. On April 9, 2026, Meta moved to dismiss the 376 Action (ECF No. 85). Meta
described Plaintiff’s allegation that a CyberTipline report had been submitted and disseminated as
“hypothetical (and elsewhere contradicted).” Meta identified the contradiction as Plaintiff’s
allegation that “Meta filed no CyberTipline report.”

36. In the 286 Action, the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report bore on
the claims then pending, including the falsity and factual basis of the statements challenged in that

action.

C. Plaintiff’s Disclosed Survivor Status

37. On September 9, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms,
Inc., et al., Case No. 3:25-cv-07671-CRB (N.D. Cal.) (the “California Action”).

38. That complaint contained a single footnote. The footnote states: “As a CSA
survivor, Plaintiff gratefully acknowledges the unwavering support of his wife, whose steady
presence made the psychological recovery, and subsequent preparation of this Complaint
possible. He further acknowledges his children, especially his eldest, who endured his distance
during the preparation of this filing after once celebrating his NRVTA graduation with pride. This
work now returns to them, just as their father and husband does.”

39. The footnote disclosed that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and had
undergone a psychological recovery that made preparation of the complaint possible.

40. Before April 22, 2026, then, Plaintiff had disclosed that he is a survivor of
childhood sexual abuse. He had described undergoing psychological recovery. He retained the
functional capacity to prepare and prosecute his pending actions.

41. The publicly filed pleadings in the 286 Action disclosed on their face that Plaintiff
is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Those pleadings alleged that placing Plaintiff’s name near
child-sexual-exploitation terminology had already caused Plaintiff emotional injury.

42. Meta, Anderson, and Keegan, through their respective counsel, received and
litigated against the 286 Action pleadings containing those disclosures before April 21, 2026.

43. The Kirkland attorneys who appeared for Accenture in the 376 Action also
represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action. They therefore possessed the 286 Action
pleadings before April 21, 2026. Accenture’s authorized representatives knew of the disclosures

before April 21, 2026.

D. CyberTipline Reporting by Meta-Operated Services
44. NCMEC receives CyberTipline reports from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
E. Counsel Operating Across Both Actions

45.  Fassbender, an attorney at Orrick, was counsel of record for Meta in the 286 Action
and for Meta and Genpact Limited in the 376 Action.

46. Chapleau and Anderson, attorneys at Kirkland, were counsel of record for
Accenture in the 376 Action. Kirkland, through Chapleau, also represented Anderson and Keegan
in the 286 Action.

47. Anderson held two roles at once. In the 286 Action he was an individual defendant
and a noticed deposition witness. In the 376 Action he was counsel of record for Accenture.

F. The Deposition Program

48. On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Accenture in
the 376 Action. The notice set a two-day examination for April 29 and April 30, 2026. Plaintiff
served the notice on Chapleau and Anderson.

49. Matter for Examination No. 5 of that notice is captioned “CyberTipline Reporting
and Reportability Status.” It encompasses “whether any CyberTipline Report was Transmitted to
NCMEC in connection with the Account-Level Enforcement Event.”

50. On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition in the 286 Action for
April 28, 2026. On April 10, 2026, Plaintiff re-served the notice with logistical details.

51. Plaintiff retained a court reporter and a videographer for the noticed depositions.

G. The April 9, 2026 Transmissions
52. On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter

captioned “Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters.” The letter

identified the 376 Action and the 286 Action by caption and case number. It enclosed copies of the
signed subpoenas Plaintiff intended to serve formally on NCMEC after the notice period had run.
It stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run.

53. Schedule A to each subpoena commanded one item: a document sufficient to show
whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1) Marvelle J.
Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.
Schedule A expressly excluded the contents of any report.

54. The April 9, 2026 transmission gave NCMEC advance notice of the subpoenas and
included copies of the signed subpoenas. Neither subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC.
Plaintiff did not request or authorize a response before formal service. Plaintiff did not waive
service. Plaintiff did not authorize NCMEC or Hall to treat receipt of the advance-notice package
as formal service.

55. On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff served the same materials under Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 45(a)(4) on counsel for the parties in both actions, including Orrick for Meta and
Kirkland for Accenture.

56. As of April 9, 2026, NCMEC had received the advance notice and its enclosures.
Counsel for Meta and counsel for Accenture had received identical materials for their clients. The
materials identified the same two federal actions, the same three identifiers, and the same
discovery objective. Each recipient knew from the face of the materials that formal service on
NCMEC was announced to occur only after the notice period had run.

57. Hall possessed or reviewed the case-specific materials no later than the moment she

approved, signed, and authorized transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters.

58. Before preparing the two case-keyed letters, Hall either reviewed the publicly filed
pleadings in the 286 Action or received from one or more participants in the two actions case-
specific materials reproducing or describing those pleadings. Those materials disclosed that
Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and described the psychological recovery that
made preparation of the California Action possible. The source, transmission, and contents of the
materials Hall reviewed or received are maintained in Defendants’ records. Plaintiff cannot reach
them without discovery.

59. Hall was Corporate Counsel of the federally designated clearinghouse for
CyberTipline reporting. She knew what it ordinarily means, in criminal and law-enforcement
terms, to associate a named individual with CyberTipline reports.

60. On the same day, April 9, 2026, Meta filed a motion to dismiss and a motion to
transfer in the 376 Action.

H. The April 21, 2026 Filings

61. On April 21, 2026, Meta, Anderson, and Keegan filed a Joint Motion to Stay
Discovery and Hold Rule 26(f) Requirements in Abeyance in the 286 Action (ECF No. 49).
Chapleau signed for Anderson and Keegan. Fassbender signed for Meta.

62. On April 21, 2026, Anderson and Keegan filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for
Protective Order in the 286 Action (ECF No. 50). The motion sought to prevent Anderson’s April
28, 2026 deposition and requested a ruling by April 24, 2026. It stated: “This motion must be
decided by April 24 because Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition on April 28, 2026.”

63. On April 21, 2026, Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and Genpact Limited filed a
Joint Motion to Stay Discovery in the 376 Action (ECF No. 92). Fassbender signed and filed the

motion for Meta and Genpact Limited. Chapleau signed with permission for Accenture. The

motion recited that Plaintiff had sought leave to serve a Request for Admission relating to
“whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account.” It stated that Plaintiff
had served “‘advance notices’ and actual notices of specific discovery that Plaintiff intends to seek
such as Rule 30(b)(6) depositions and third-party subpoenas.”

64. On April 21, 2026, Accenture filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for Protective Order in
the 376 Action (ECF No. 93). The motion sought to prevent the April 29-30, 2026 Rule 30(b)(6)
deposition and requested a ruling by April 27, 2026. Accenture attached the deposition notice,
including Matter for Examination No. 5, as Exhibit 1. The motion stated: “This time-sensitive
motion must be decided by April 27 because Plaintiff noticed Accenture’s deposition for April 29-
30.”

65. The April 21, 2026 motions sought relief reaching the Anderson deposition, the
Accenture Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, and Plaintiff’s contemplated third-party discovery. Neither
court had ruled on any of them.

66. Neither April 21, 2026 joint motion—in the 376 Action or the 286 Action—
identified any forthcoming response from NCMEC.

I. The April 22, 2026 Letters: Issuance Before Formal Service

67. On April 22, 2026, Hall issued two letters on NCMEC letterhead. That was one day
after the filings described in Section H. It was thirteen days after NCMEC received the advance-
notice package. It was before formal service of either subpoena. Each letter was keyed by caption
and case number to one of the two federal actions. One letter bears on its face Case No. 6:26-cv-
00376-AGM-DCI. The other bears on its face Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI. Two letters,
each keyed to a separate action, reflect the processing of two separate matters under two specific

captions and case numbers.

68. The two letters are identical in substantive text. This Complaint refers to “the April
22, 2026 letter” to mean the content the two letters share. Each letter identified Plaintiff by the
names “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and “Jay Ballentine” and by the email address
jaychizza@icloud.com.

69. The letter opened with this sentence: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9,
2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written
responses as detailed below.”

70. Neither subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC in connection with
Plaintiff. No process server had delivered a subpoena to NCMEC. No subpoena return, proof of
service, certificate of service, or process-server affidavit existed. No court order required Hall or
NCMEC to respond. The announced notice period had not run.

71. When the letters issued, none of the April 21, 2026 motions had been decided.
Neither court had ruled on any motion to stay discovery or any motion for protective order. The
ruling dates the movants themselves had requested had not arrived: April 24, 2026 in the 286
Action, April 27, 2026 in the 376 Action.

72. Hall did not wait for formal service of any subpoena. Hall did not wait for the courts
to rule on the pending motions.

73. Every requested ruling date and every noticed deposition fell after April 22, 2026.
The 286 Action ruling date fell two days after the letters issued. The 376 Action ruling date fell
five days after. The Anderson deposition was set for April 28, 2026, six days after. The Accenture
Rule 30(b)(6) deposition was set for April 29 and 30, 2026, seven and eight days after. No rule,

order, or obligation required Hall to issue the letters before any of those dates.

74. On April 27, 2026, the magistrate judge in the 286 Action granted the motion for
protective order and temporarily stayed discovery. On April 30, 2026, the magistrate judge in the
376 Action entered a report recommending that the joint motion to stay discovery be granted (ECF
No. 103). On May 1, 2026, the magistrate judge in the 376 Action granted Accenture’s motion for
protective order and ordered: “Discovery is temporarily stayed pending resolution of the motion to
stay discovery” (ECF No. 104).

75. The letter did not produce the document Schedule A described. It stated instead:
“NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay
Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022
and the present.”

76. The three identifiers stated in the letter were quoted from Plaintiff’s own April 9,
2026 notice.

77. Each letter was addressed to Plaintiff alone, at his commercial mail-receiving
address in Alexandria, Virginia. Neither letter bore any notation that it was copied to any court or
counsel of record. Neither letter was filed in either action.

78. Neither letter was a CyberTipline report. Neither was a referral or disclosure to any
law-enforcement agency. Neither was made under, or implemented, any reporting, preservation,
referral, or disclosure function described in 18 U.S.C. §§ 2258A, 2258B, or 2258C. Each letter
was voluntary correspondence. It issued after signed subpoenas existed, before formal service of
either, and in the absence of any court order or other legal obligation. The challenged conduct did
not arise from the performance of any responsibility or function described in 18 U.S.C. §
2258D(a), 18 U.S.C. §§ 2258A or 2258C, or 34 U.S.C. § 11293. It was not undertaken as part of

any effort to identify a child victim. In the alternative, the conduct alleged was intentional, was

undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal
justification, and served a purpose unrelated to any responsibility or function identified in 18
U.S.C. § 2258D(a).

79.  Hall was NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she drafted, signed, and transmitted
the letters. She signed both in the course of her work at NCMEC’s Alexandria, Virginia
headquarters.

80. As Corporate Counsel, Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC
issued in response to claimed legal process.

81. On information and belief, NCMEC keeps ordinary legal-intake records sufficient
to show whether a subpoena has been served on it.

82. On information and belief, Hall reviewed or had access to those records, and they
were sufficient to tell her, before issuance, that no subpoena had been served on NCMEC.

83.  Hall’s signature appears on each letter. Each letter identifies Hall as the sender.

84. Hall controlled or approved the wording of the letters. Hall selected the language
characterizing them as a response to a subpoena. Hall authorized their transmission.

85. Hall drafted and transmitted the letters anyway.

86. Before drafting, signing, and transmitting the letters, Hall reviewed or had access to
the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI and the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-
AGM-DCI.

87. Hall had reason to know that each docket contained publicly filed claims brought by
Plaintiff. Hall had reason to know that the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI
contained publicly filed claims predicated on the linkage of Plaintiff’s name to child-sexual-

exploitation terminology.

88. Hall has not withdrawn, corrected, or retracted either letter. Hall has instead
affirmatively defended the letters as accurate and proper.

J. The April 22, 2026 Letters: Content Defects

89. The letter identified no report number, no report date, and no reporting electronic
service provider.

90. The letter did not state that Meta submitted either report. It did not state that either
report concerned Plaintiff’s Facebook account. It did not state that either report concerned Meta’s
July 4, 2022 contract interference.

91. The letter joined Plaintiff’s three identifiers with “and/or.” It did not establish that
any single identifier corresponded to either report.

92. The letter included no custodian-of-records declaration and no certification under
Federal Rule of Evidence 902(11) or 902(12).

93. The name “Jay Ballentine,” standing alone, does not uniquely identify anyone. The
letter did not state that NCMEC used any disambiguation process to determine that a CyberTipline
report associated with that name concerned Plaintiff rather than another person of the same or
similar name.

94. The letter did not state whether “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “Jay Ballentine,” or
jaychizza@icloud.com appeared in any CyberTipline report, in any electronic-service-provider
submission, or in NCMEC’s internal records, or whether those identifiers were derived from any
source independent of the letter itself.

95. The letter did not state that NCMEC had determined that “Marvelle J. Ballentine,”

“Jay Ballentine,” and jaychizza@icloud.com refer to the same person.

96. Schedule A stated the period “July 2, 2022 through the date of compliance.” The
letters stated the period “July 1, 2022 and the present.”

97. Schedule A referred to any “CyberTipline report, referral, or submission.” The
letters stated that NCMEC had received “two (2) CyberTipline reports.”

98. The letters listed “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “Jay Ballentine,” and
jaychizza@icloud.com in the same order in which Plaintiff listed them in the April 9 materials.

K. Statutory Imputation and Defamatory Meaning

99. Section 2258A of Title 18 requires an electronic service provider to report to
NCMEC’s CyberTipline after obtaining actual knowledge of facts or circumstances from which
there is an apparent violation of specified federal child-exploitation statutes. The CyberTipline
also receives reports from other sources concerning suspected child exploitation.

100. The statutes enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A include 18 U.S.C. § 2251 (sexual
exploitation of children), § 2251A (selling or buying of children), § 2252 (certain activities
relating to material involving the sexual exploitation of minors), § 2252A (certain activities
relating to material constituting or containing child pornography), and § 2422(b) (coercion and
enticement of minors).

101. In the context alleged, a reader of the letter would understand the statement that
NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports “concerning” Plaintiff’s full legal name and
identifiers to convey that NCMEC had received two reports associating Plaintiff personally with
suspected child-exploitation conduct and that the reported matter could be made available to law

enforcement.

102. By linking Plaintiff’s full legal name to two CyberTipline reports, the letter imputes
to Plaintiff conduct constituting offenses involving moral turpitude. If the imputation were true,
Plaintiff could be indicted and punished for those offenses.

103. The imputation is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct constituting, or
reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

L. Transmission, Publication, and Continuing Exposure
